title: Computer Networks (deep)
summary: Every backend request travels through layers, addresses, and congestion control you can't see — until you can, and half your weird-latency mysteries solve themselves.

blocks.markdown:
A network is just machines agreeing on rules to find each other and pass bytes.

- Data is **chunked into packets**, each stamped with a destination **IP address**.
- **Routers** forward packets one **hop** at a time — no router knows the whole path.
- The core stays dumb and fast; **reliability lives at the endpoints** (the end-to-end principle).
- **TCP** rebuilds a clean, in-order byte stream from a lossy, reordering network.

blocks.subTitle: Pick a transport
blocks.markdown:
Choose your transport by what your app does with a late packet.

| Need | Reach for |
|---|---|
| Reliable, ordered bytes | TCP |
| Low latency, loss OK | UDP |
| HTTP without HOL blocking | QUIC (HTTP/3) |
| Split a network into subnets | CIDR / subnetting |

blocks.subTitle: The layers
blocks.markdown:
Layering splits networking into jobs, each talking only to its neighbours.

- **OSI** is a 7-layer teaching map; **TCP/IP** is the 4 layers the internet actually runs.
- **Link** moves a frame one hop (MAC addresses). **Internet/IP** moves a packet end to end (IP addresses), no reliability promise.
- **Transport/TCP** adds reliability, ordering, and **ports**. **Application** is your data and its meaning.
- "Layer 7 LB" = OSI application; "Layer 4 LB" = transport. Knowing both numbering schemes is an interview staple.

blocks.subTitle: Encapsulation
blocks.markdown:
Going down the stack, each layer wraps the data in its own header — nested envelopes.

![TCP/IP layers and encapsulation](assets/computer-networks/osi-tcpip-encapsulation.svg)

- App data becomes a **TCP segment** (ports, seq, ACK), then an **IP packet** (src/dst IP, TTL), then an **Ethernet frame** (MACs + checksum).
- Each layer treats the one above as **opaque payload** — IP carries TCP without understanding it.
- The receiver strips headers in reverse. The **destination IP and ports are buried inside**; the outer MAC only matters for the next hop.

blocks.subTitle: IP addresses & CIDR
blocks.markdown:
An IPv4 address is 32 bits split into a **network part** and a **host part**.

- **CIDR** `/n` says the first `n` bits are the network; the rest are hosts. `10.0.1.0/24` gives 256 addresses, 254 usable.
- Same subnet? **Bitwise-AND** both addresses with the mask and compare. Same network = talk directly at the link layer; else go through a **router**.
- **Private** ranges (`10/8`, `172.16/12`, `192.168/16`) aren't public-routable; **NAT** rewrites them at the edge.
- **IPv6** uses 128-bit addresses, ending exhaustion and largely removing NAT.

blocks.subTitle: Routing hop by hop
blocks.markdown:
Each router forwards a packet one hop closer using its routing table.

![A packet routed hop by hop](assets/computer-networks/packet-routing-hops.svg)

- **Longest-prefix match**: pick the most specific prefix containing the destination IP; fall back to the **default route** `0.0.0.0/0`.
- The router rewrites the **MAC header** for the next hop but leaves the **destination IP fixed**, and decrements **TTL** by one (zero = dropped, kills loops).
- Tables fill via **OSPF/IS-IS** inside an org and **BGP** between orgs — a BGP slip took Facebook offline in 2021.

blocks.subTitle: TCP reliability
blocks.markdown:
TCP turns lossy IP into a reliable, ordered byte stream.

- **Three-way handshake** (SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK) agrees to talk and swaps initial sequence numbers — costs **one full RTT** before data.
- TCP numbers every **byte**; ACKs are **cumulative** ("got everything up to N"). A gap makes the receiver repeat a **duplicate ACK**.
- **Retransmit** on timeout (RTO), or faster on **3 duplicate ACKs** (fast retransmit). **SACK** resends only the gaps.
- The **sliding window** sends many unacked bytes at once: throughput ≈ **window / RTT**.

blocks.subTitle: Congestion control
blocks.markdown:
Flow control protects the receiver; **congestion control** protects the shared network.

![TCP congestion window over time](assets/computer-networks/tcp-congestion-control.svg)

- Sender is bounded by `min(rwnd, cwnd)`. **rwnd** = receiver's free buffer; **cwnd** = network estimate.
- **Slow start** doubles cwnd each RTT (exponential — only the *start* is small) until ssthresh or loss.
- **AIMD**: additive increase (+1 segment/RTT), multiplicative decrease (halve on loss) — the sawtooth. Loss is the congestion signal.
- **BBR** models bandwidth and RTT instead of reacting to loss — far better on lossy wireless links.

blocks.subTitle: UDP
blocks.markdown:
UDP is TCP's minimalist cousin: just **ports** and an optional checksum over IP.

- No handshake, no sequence numbers, no ACKs, no retransmit, no ordering, no congestion control. Header is **8 bytes** vs TCP's 20+.
- You send a **datagram** and hope. That buys low latency and no **head-of-line blocking**.
- Great for **DNS** (one tiny query), live media, and games — where a late packet is useless anyway.
- "Unreliable" means a **blank canvas**, not unimportant: **QUIC** rebuilds reliability over UDP, per stream.

blocks.subTitle: TCP vs UDP
blocks.markdown:
Both ride on IP; they trade reliability against latency.

| Aspect | TCP | UDP |
|---|---|---|
| Setup | Handshake (1 RTT) | None |
| Delivery | Reliable, ordered | Best-effort |
| On loss | Retransmit, stall | Skip it |
| Header | 20+ bytes | 8 bytes |

Lean TCP when a late byte still matters; lean UDP (or QUIC) when stale data is worthless.

blocks.subTitle: The core tensions
blocks.markdown:
A few physics-bound trade-offs shape every network decision.

- **Throughput vs RTT** — capped by `window / RTT`; on a long fat pipe you need **window scaling** or bandwidth is wasted.
- **Latency floor** — light is ~1ms per 100 miles; you can't optimise it away, only move data closer ([caching](caching), CDNs).
- **Connection cost vs reuse** — each TCP connection pays a handshake + slow-start ramp, so **keep-alive / pooling** beats reopening.
- **Address space vs reach** — IPv4 + NAT saves addresses but breaks end-to-end; IPv6 restores it.

blocks.subTitle: Real systems
blocks.markdown:
Networking trade-offs show up as products and defaults.

- **HTTP/3 + QUIC** — over UDP, orders **per stream** so one lost packet doesn't stall the rest; folds in TLS for 1-RTT (or 0-RTT).
- **CDNs** terminate TCP **close to the user** to shrink RTT, and use BGP **anycast** to route to the nearest edge.
- **Linux** defaults to **CUBIC**; Google runs **BBR** to avoid mistaking wireless loss for congestion.
- **DNS** uses UDP on port 53 first, falling back to **TCP** for large responses.

The misconceptions that bite in interviews and on-call:

- **"More bandwidth fixes slow transfers."** For small objects on high-RTT links, **round trips dominate** — CDNs beat fatter pipes.
- **"Slow start is slow."** Growth is exponential; only the initial window is small.
- **"Flow control = congestion control."** rwnd protects the **receiver**; cwnd protects the **network**.
- **"An IP identifies a device."** It marks an interface's **location** — it can change (DHCP) or be shared (NAT); MACs identify hardware.
- **"A bigger mask means more hosts."** Backwards — more network bits means **fewer** hosts per subnet.
